prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map captures the smooth gradient of the asphalt roadway and right-hand raised curb stretching from roughly 1–2 metres at the bottom of the view out to an intersection over 15–30 metres ahead, with nothing within arm's reach of the camera wearer. In frames 1 and 2, a cyclist on the right sidewalk corner is visible as a silhouette about 8–10 metres away facing right (with the bicycle within the cyclist's reach) in front of more distant background cars (15–25 metres away), before the camera pitches down and turns left onto the bike lane pavement in frame 3. In frames 4 and 5, as the camera turns left and then back right toward the intersection, a pedestrian walking rightward across the road appears at roughly 12–15 metres away (about 4–5 metres in front of and to the left of a pickup truck in frame 4, and 15+ metres to the left of the right-side curb and vehicles in frame 5). The depth map highlights the 3D step of the nearby right curb and separates the foreground cyclist and pedestrian from the background intersection clutter better than RGB alone, though it fails to resolve the cyclists' thin wheel spokes and renders the distant sky, overhead traffic lights, and far horizon (>20 metres) as uniformly black.
descriptions.segmentation: The instance segmentation map isolates and labels discrete traffic participants and infrastructure—specifically overhead traffic lights (roughly 15–25 metres away and high above the road), distant cars (15–35 metres away), a cyclist (`person` and `bicycle`) on the right corner at 8–10 metres in frames 1–2, and a walking `person` plus a `truck` at 12–20 metres in frames 4–5. In frames 1 and 2, the cyclist is positioned to the right in front of partially occluded background cars while facing right and away from the camera wearer, whereas in frames 4 and 5 a pedestrian walks left-to-right across the street (facing right in profile, not looking at the camera wearer) ahead of a pickup truck that becomes mostly cut off at the right edge of frame 5. Nothing is within arm's reach of the camera wearer in any frame, and only the bicycle is within reach of the cyclist in frames 1–2. This map makes tiny, low-contrast distant vehicles and high overhead traffic signals much easier to spot and count than in the raw RGB image, but it is completely blank during the downward head tilt in frame 3, splits the bicycle into disconnected wheel masks, and misses several background cars and static road features like curbs and poles.
descriptions.pose: The pose map is completely black across all 5 frames, detecting no body or hand skeletons anywhere in the scene. In the RGB strip, the only people present—the cyclist on the right curb in frames 1–2 (about 8–10 metres away, facing right with hands on the handlebars) and the pedestrian crossing left-to-right in frames 4–5 (about 12–15 metres away, facing right in profile and not looking toward the camera wearer)—are too distant and small in image resolution for the pose estimator to register. Neither the camera wearer's own body/hands nor any person within arm's reach (under 1 metre) enters the field of view, even when the camera pitches sharply down toward the painted bike-lane pavement in frame 3. Consequently, the pose map provides no spatial information beyond confirming the absence of close-range people, making it entirely unreliable for tracking the distant cyclist and pedestrian visible in the RGB frames.
